title: Metrons & Logons: Morgane Billuart in Conversation with Matthew Johnstone
content:
Metrons and Logons brings together Matthew’s recent series of photographic works with display structures made by eva duerden. The images move between recognisable objects and architecturally processed surfaces, reminding us of objects we used to consider technical, while acknowledging their obsolescence. The longer one looks, the less clear that designation of time becomes. The result is a set of images that seem familiar but increasingly difficult to place, inviting the viewer to stare at pictures with an intrigued, yet suspicious eye. In this conversation, Matthew Johnstone and Morgane Billuart discuss what happens to an image when it unknowingly appears to be a testimony of a world that breaks down, and yet, perhaps, with another life force, an odd gaze, is starting anew.

Matthew Johnstone,  Repose_8176, 2025. Archival C-type print, PVC, Metrons & Logons, Turning Space, Berlin, 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Turning Space

Morgane

Matthew, in the show Metrons and Logons, what am I seeing exactly?

Matthew

Good question.

title: Digital Diogenes or If I Stay Here, Something Precious in Me Will Die
content:
It’s been a long time since images stopped being sacred. They are simply one of the millions of scraps in which I melt.

I am everywhere and everything that can be. And yet I am in a place: this sort of cage called identity, built of fake nostalgia and estrangement from myself. And if I stay here, something precious in me will die.

I dissolve into all the fragments of myself I have chosen to accumulate. The photographs I keep on my phone are not decisions, but rather an unconscious extension of my identity. I am what is worth looking at and, above all, what is worth not deleting.

When I take a photo, or save an image because I find it funny, I do so not as an act of significance, but as a mechanical one because that’s the way of existing online.

creator: Júlia Serra

title: Digital Tribulations 25: Building Technological Sovereignty from Below, The Experience of Argentine Cooperativism – Interview with Cecilia Muñoz from Código Libre
content:
The introduction of Digital Tribulations, a series of intellectual interviews on the developments of digital sovereignty in Latin America, can be read here and the entire series can be found here.

During the month I spent in Buenos Aires, the last city I visited before finally flying back to Europe, I managed to get a firsthand look at its famous cooperativist scene, which extends to platforms. By “famous” I of course mean a niche that has accompanied platform studies since the sharing economy: platform cooperativism. I first came across it through the pioneering work of Trebor Scholz, and I became more familiar with it thanks to the prolific scholarship of my Brazilian friend Rafael Grohmann. He was the one who gave me Cecilia’s contact, along with the phone number of a fellow Italian, Stefano Tortorici, who is writing his PhD on platform cooperativism. As two Italian researchers in our semi-nomadic phase, I bonded with Stefano and ended up hanging out with his numerous artistic housemates, who shared a house not far from the gentrified Palermo neighborhood.

title: From the Autistici/Inventati Case to a European Dispute over Financial Autonomy
content:
We have drafted a proposal: can the European Commission protect Autistici/Inventati from the effects of the sanctions imposed by the Trump administration? We have spoken with lawyers, involved several Members of Parliament, and we know that there is a legal avenue to protect European citizens, organisations and banks from the extraterritorial effects of these sanctions. But legal instruments need to be matched by the political force required to use them.

Banca Etica, by contrast, continues to argue that fighting to make this happen is not its responsibility and that its priority is simply to protect itself. Ilaria Salis and Benedetta Scuderi are already taking action in the European Parliament, but the road will be long. I firmly believe that this is not the time to remain indifferent.

In a September in which far-right forces continue to advance in Germany, and in which the United States is placing people and organisations committed to antifascism and the defence of rights on a blacklist, despite there being no judicial conviction against them in Italy or the European Union, the response cannot be: let it go, better not to raise our heads too much.

title: Digital Tribulations 24: Perspectives of Digital Liberation in Latin America Between Dependency, Labor, and Automation – Interview with Juan Martin Graña
content:
The introduction of Digital Tribulations, a series of intellectual interviews on the developments of digital sovereignty in Latin America, can be read here and the entire series can be found here.

I met Juan Martín Graña, a CONICET researcher, one morning in early April in Buenos Aires, at a café called Aromi, near Parque Centenario, in the Caballito neighborhood. We were put in touch by Cecilia Rikap, who recently published the book Teoría de la Dependencia Digital, so far only available in Spanish, and whose book presentation, held at the public School of Economics of the UBA, I attended in a packed room. 

Juan and I sat down at a large round table, ordered the inevitable coffee and medialunas, and began talking for about an hour about the political economy of digital dependency in Latin America. Over the course of the long conversation, Juan Martín laid out a framework that challenges mainstream narratives about automation and job loss in the Global South, arguing that the real risk is not mass unemployment but a deepening technological gap that translates into low wages and precarious work.

title: Streaming after Instantaneity
content:
Speech at INC Exit Fest, OT 301, Amsterdam, 25th June, 2026.

Online video has become the general condition of social media, a streaming vortex driven by extractivism and behavioural targeting. Reflecting on my experience as a member of CDI-TV,[1] a collective contributing to StreamArtNetwork (SAN), I want to consider this condition from a specific angle, what I am calling poor chroma: the shimmering, unstable borders that appear where chroma-keyed bodies fail to seamlessly converge with the background, where a slight glitched-out halo forms around hair and fingers, the signs of a spill that doesn’t quite wash out. They might seem like minor technical imperfections, but I argue that poor chroma offers one way to understand the stakes of streaming in terms of tactical publishing, strategic power and the logistical operations of streaming infrastructures. Poor chroma can help us understand how liveness, distribution and collectivity are both held together and apart by corporate stacks; in other words, how they are interfaced and, therefore, how the mediation within the vortex becomes conceivable.[2]

THE UNSTABLE OBJECT
snippet: Speech at INC Exit Fest, OT 301, Amsterdam, 25th June, 2026.
creator: Michael Dieter

title: Digital Tribulations 23: Let’s Talk About Digital Sovereignty in Latin American Governments – Interview with Luis Papagni
content:
The introduction of Digital Tribulations, a series of intellectual interviews on the developments of digital sovereignty in Latin America, can be read here. The entire series can be found here.

Esteban from the AGC (Asociación Gremial de Computación) — Argentina’s tech worker union — invited me to the first meeting of the informatical workers of Argentina. It was held at the UMET, Universidad Metropolitana para la Educación y el Trabajo, founded in 2013, and currently co-managed by more than 100 unions, civil society groups, and municipalities, which shape its degree programs and research agendas around the country’s productive and technological development. UMET runs a joint research center with CONICET, Argentina’s national scientific council, focused on work, technology, and social innovation. It offers subsidized tuition for union members and their families as part of a push to widen access to higher education for workers. The meeting ran from 6pm, with a light reception at the entrance: the coffee was bad, but the medialunas were good. There were associations coming from all around the country.

title: *Out Now* Art, Activism, Academia: Changemaking in Contemporary Amsterdam
content:
The Institute of Network Cultures is proud to present the first publication of its last intern at HvA, Noah Pellikaan, produced at INC in the first half of 2026:

Art, Activism, Academia: Changemaking in Contemporary Amsterdam is a collected, fragmentary volume speaking on left-wing social movements in Amsterdam’s artistic and academic spheres, with an emphasis on the 2015-2024 period. This book contains writings and interviews of varying literary style and formula, with collaborators across and surpassing fields of academic, political, and artistic practice. It’s lessons are resultant from Amsterdam, yes, though applicable far beyond it. The intent of Art, Activism, Academia is that of the generative archive, to create and curate activistic memory so as to intervene toward a better today.

title: Flat World Theory
content:
(expanded version of talk given at the opening evening of INC Exit Fest at UvA Spui25 in Amsterdam, June 22, 2026)

Tonight, I would like to cast the idea of flat world theory to you and introduce the concept of the logistical episteme. Flat world theory – this is not to be confused with the Latourian world of flat ontologies where conflictual confrontations of the political evaporate into a chain of empty signifiers and relational assemblages. But we might be talking about what Anna Kornbluh in her critique of the immediacy of style in too-late capitalism calls “Knausgaard’s acid-brilliant flat ontology: everything is everything.”[1] To be sure, everything is everything is just another variation of flat ontologies. It’s the acid-brilliance that unsettles the order of things.

Flat world theory takes the world for what it is in the logistical age of AI: flat as a mat.

title: Let’s Play Image Type Charades!
content:
Proceedings from my presentation during EXIT FEST on the 24th of June 2026, in celebration of Geert Lovink and the Institute of Network Cultures’ departure from the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences (HvA) on September 1, 2026.

The Digital Image is Non-Static

While we usually think of images as static objects, they are in fact never completely stable. Processing, use, and semiotics may all affect the life of the image: a photograph may exist as a momentary render, while also becoming evidence, or a symbol, depending on how, where, and by whom it is used or seen.

title: Body is a Lost Media, Pixels Are All You’re Gonna See – Reframing the Blur and the Body Across Palestine Online
content:
I remember scrolling the Instagram account @eyeonpalestine for months, and how you start to feel like when you stay there long enough and become doomed by a sensation, becoming a fog. The feeling is both physical and emotional. It’s like being somewhere after an explosion. You got blurry vision, your ears are buzzing.

Some images are clear, unfiltered, and painful as they were meant to be: bodies, rubble, blood. Others are covered. Blurred. There is apparently no legible criteria, no consistent logic you can extract from what gets blurred and what does not. Extremely violent images sometimes appear in full while others, less graphic, less explicit, are swallowed by a grey screen, a pixelated veil, and a sign that resembles a blinded eye, an eye with an arrow upon it. The signs of what Instagram calls “sensitive content warning.”

From Exactly That Body: Images Against Oppression, Kateryna Iakovlenko, e-flux Journal, Issue #133

title: Duckrabbits Talk Back #5: Hegemony and Complexity w/ Nora Sternfeld
content:
What is really political art? What is the relation between art and hegemony? And how to be an uncompromising antifascist in a complex, multipolar world? To discuss these deep question, we are joined by Nora Sternfeld, an independent curator and Professor of Art Education at the University of Fine Arts in Hamburg. Expect no clear-cut, simple answers, but in-depth discussions about the opposition between simplistic complexity and complex simplicity, para-institutionality, counter-monuments, sober coalition-building, and the notion of propaganda. Please join us in the labyrinth of concepts, because it will be worth your while.

title: Report: Creative Resistance Against AI Assembly
content:
Friday June 26 we organized a Creative Resistance Against AI Assembly during the INC Exit Fest. Some of you were there. It was hot, it started a bit too late, we might not have properly invited everyone, and honestly: we pretty much improvised on the spot because of the circumstances. But we loved to do it, we met some great people, and we want to just share with you that it happened and that it will happen again later! We decided to continue exchange and collaboration around creative resistance to current tech systems.

Below a small recap with some links to materials that were shared. We took resisting and refusing AI as an inherently collective, defiantly promising, and inherently creative field of research and experimentation.

At 10 o’clock in the morning we gathered at the OT301 in Amsterdam, it was more than 30 degrees Celsius, and we already had an evening and full day of great talks and nice people. But we were determined to go ahead with it and take our time to discuss and find common threads.

title: Digital Tribulations 22: Argentina’s Tech Workers Union After Milei and AI: an Interview with AGC
content:
The introduction of Digital Tribulations, a series of intellectual interviews on the developments of digital sovereignty in Latin America, can be read here and the entire serie can be found here.

When I arrived in Argentina in March 2026, my friend Simone Robutti, a political organiser with Tech Workers Coalition based in Berlin, had put me in contact with Esteban from AGC (Asociación Gremial de Computación). A gremio is the specific Argentine term for a trade union, which, besides negotiating wages, does all sorts of activities: managing their members’ healthcare, owning recreational facilities, running vocational training centres, and more. They function, in practice, as a parallel welfare state organised by sector. With the nice weather of the end of the summer, I walked into the union building in the centre of Buenos Aires. As I went upstairs, I was welcomed with coffee, and we sat around the table in the AGC’s meeting room.
